title: Meghan's father Thomas Markle detained for allegedly cutting off ankle monitor, officials say
description: Thomas Markle, the father of Meghan, Duchess of Sussex, has been detained in Florida for allegedly removing his ankle monitor, according to justice de
body: Thomas Markle, the father of Meghan, Duchess of Sussex, has been detained in Florida for allegedly removing his ankle monitor, according to justice department officials in Los Angeles.Markle appeared before a federal magistrate judge in the Florida city of Tampa after allegedly removing the monitor at 01:45 local time (06:45 GMT), a justice department (DoJ) spokesperson told the BBC.The judge ordered him jailed without bond and he is now in federal custody, the spokesperson said. Markle, who has previously denied possessing images of child sex abuse, was arrested in Florida last week and placed under house detention. He was also ordered to wear a location monitoring device. The BBC has contacted his representatives.US Judge Lindsay S Griffin said on Tuesday that Markle's housing situation "had become untenable", according to court documents. Griffin cited a "lack of suitable housing", writing in the order that "no condition or combination of conditions would reasonably assure the safety of any other person or the community and the defendant's appearance in court".He also ordered a medical evaluation for Markle and said he "must receive all necessary and prescribed medication unless discontinued by a physician"."Release conditions are court orders, not suggestions," Bill Essayli, the US attorney for Central California, wrote on X on Tuesday about Markle's alleged removal of his ankle monitor."We will continue to prosecute this case to the fullest extent of the law," Essayli added.Markle was first arrested last week after the FBI, acting on warrants, searched storage units in Los Angeles registered to him which he had rented since 2008, with the last payment being made in October this year, the DoJ said.Inside the units the FBI says agents seized about 78 items, including film negatives, slides and books that they allege contained child sex abuse material.Witnesses "positively identified" Markle in two of the images believed to contain child sex abuse material.In those images, the man pictured "appears to be in the age range of 30s to 40s", which suggests the alleged abuse dates back decades as Markle is currently 82 years old.Markle appeared in court last week following his arrest. No plea was taken during the appearance, which set several conditions for his pretrial release, including that he be kept in home detention. He is charged with one count of possessing indecent images of children, according to the DoJ.FBI director Kash Patel said last week that Markle "allegedly targeted innocent children and sought to steal their innocence through his criminal actions".Markle has called the allegations "sick lies".He moved to the Philippines last year after he had a series of strokes, and lived in Cebu until May. He was reportedly learning to walk again in Florida after having his leg amputated.The duchess has been estranged from her father since 2018. The BBC understands she broke contact with him last year, telling him she and the authorities knew he had abused young girls.In a previously shared statement, Meghan confirmed the existence of the letter and wrote: "I am deeply distressed... my thoughts are with any children who may have been harmed."She said she hoped it could be understood why she had largely cut off contact from her father and did "not allow him to have contact with our children".

schema.headline: Meghan's father Thomas Markle detained for allegedly cutting off ankle monitor, officials say

title: Spain's king and queen attend memorial service for rail crash victims
description: Spain's King Felipe and Queen Letizia were among those who have attended a memorial service in tribute to the 69 victims of last month's deadly train
body: Spain's King Felipe and Queen Letizia were among those who have attended a memorial service in tribute to the 69 victims of last month's deadly train crash.The accident occurred when one train, travelling at high speed, ploughed into the back of another that was stationary on the Madrid-Seville line, near the small town of Urda, about 40 miles from Toledo.It was the worst rail tragedy in Spain since 2013. Twenty-eight people remain in hospital."The tragic accident in Urda has left our families, our towns and our society with a pain that is difficult to accept," Archbishop Cerro Chaves told those present.Representatives of those killed carried lit candles to the front of the cathedral and placed them next to the main altar. The first reading of the service was by Ana Benítez, sister of David Benítez, a 38-year-old father-of-two who died.The king and queen were met with applause by bystanders as they entered the cathedral and at the end of the service, after Catholic Mass, they spoke to relatives of the victims.Senior politicians also attended the service, including the leader of the opposition People's Party, Alberto Núñez Feijóo, the president of the Castilla-La Mancha region, Emiliano García-Page, and Transport and Economy Minister Carlos Cuerpo. Cuerpo took on the transport portfolio following the resignation last week of Óscar Puente from the post.

schema.headline: Spain's king and queen attend memorial service for rail crash victims

title: David Walliams accused of sexual misconduct in Guardian and ITN investigation
description: David Walliams accused of sexual misconduct after losing injunction bidFigure caption, Woman accusing Walliams of grooming speaks to BBC NewsnightBySt
body: David Walliams accused of sexual misconduct after losing injunction bidFigure caption, Woman accusing Walliams of grooming speaks to BBC NewsnightBySteven McIntoshUpdated 1 hour agoITV News and the Guardian have published reports alleging that David Walliams has been accused of sexual misconduct by several women, including one who was aged 15.The allegations were made as a part of a joint three-year investigation, external by the two news organisations, which was published after the entertainer lost a legal bid to stop the claims against him being made public.Some of the women accuse Walliams of "grooming" them when they were teenagers. One now characterises her alleged encounter with Walliams at 15-years- old as a "sexual assault".In a letter to journalists published by the Guardian, Walliams said he was "not a sexual predator" and had not "broken the law".He said he "realised that at times I behaved thoughtlessly towards other people I had casual sexual relationships with" and said he regretted not always taking "people's feelings properly into account".If you are affected by any of the issues in this story, help and support is available at BBC Action Line.Image source, Getty ImagesWalliams shot to fame alongside Matt Lucas in the early 2000s with BBC sketch comedy Little Britain, and also served as a judge on ITV's Britain's Got Talent and launched a best-selling series of children's books. The Guardian and ITV News say that several of the women, who do not know one another, allege they were targets of unwanted sexual advances from Walliams.The allegations include:One woman alleges she met Walliams at a fan event when she was 15. She says he groomed her and they had sex when she was 17Another woman alleges she met Walliams for a coffee when she was 15, before going back to his house where he allegedly tried to lift up her shirt and commit an act that she now describes as a sexual assaultA woman who worked as a model in her teens accused Walliams of grooming her. A different woman who also worked as a model said Walliams tried to kiss her while showing her around his homeThe investigation claimed Walliams had a sexual relationship with at least one junior employee at publisher HarperCollins, and pursued anotherOther women allege inappropriate behaviour at ITV's Britain's Got Talent, such as inviting girls and young women to his dressing roomIn a letter addressed to journalists working on the ITV and Guardian investigation, Walliams wrote: "Looking back, I realise that at times I behaved thoughtlessly towards other people I had casual sexual relationships with."I realise I did not always take people's feelings properly into account. That is something I regret. And whilst a power imbalance is inevitable when one party is famous, abusing that power is something else entirely and it is something that I never did."He added: "I am not a sexual predator. I have not broken the law, but I am devastated that some of the women I met 10 to 20 years ago have now expressed hurt or anger towards me."After the investigation was published on Tuesday, Walliams's long-time literary agent Independent Talent Group confirmed it had dropped him.A BBC spokesperson described the allegations as "serious" and the corporation has removed Little Britain from BBC iPlayer. Sky also described the allegations as "extremely serious", saying it was dropping its upcoming adaptation of Walliams's fantasy feature Fing! and had "already removed content which features him from our platforms".The Metropolitan Police said it has contacted the Guardian and ITV News to "to ensure that any potential victims" are "made aware of how they could report any criminal allegations to police".Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Walliams (right, with Matt Lucas, in 2006) shot to fame on the BBC comedy sketch series Little BritainOne of the women who alleged Walliams "groomed" her as a teenager told BBC Newsnight she was "angry" at his behaviour.Lilly Creightmore - who Walliams contacted when she was 18 - waived her right to anonymity.Creightmore told Newsnight that a month after they first met, Walliams told her she "could move in with him and basically that I could be his flatmate".She said that after she arrived to stay at his house she "felt instantly pressured to share a bed with him"."In the evenings, he would sort of come and sit with me and stroke my leg, and one night I think he put his head in my lap and sort of be like, 'are you sure you don't want to come and sleep in my bed with me?' I had an inner strength like, 'no I'm not attracted to you in that way'... I felt I was being manipulated," she added.She told Newsnight: "I am angry, I'm suppressing it well, but just that this culture of older men in positions of power needs to go, needs to stop. They're abusing their positions, using young people and abusing young people, and people of any age of course. There were too many men in power still, that are doing this and they need to go."Walliams's lawyers told the ITV News and Guardian investigation that he denied grooming Creightmore or acting inappropriately. They added he did not "target" her because she was "vulnerable" or "young".Walliams said he believed his friendship with Lilly was a "special one" and felt "devastated" by her account. He denied the offers of help or gifts were attempts to groom, manipulate or coerce her into sleeping with him.Two women, given pseudonyms of Alex and Jade in the investigation, have alleged that they first had contact with Walliams when they were 15 years old.Alex alleged that she met Walliams in 2004 at a fan event when she was 15. She claimed that she and Walliams stayed in touch over the next two years and they had consensual sex for the first time when she was 17, the report alleged.Figure caption, 'I think I was groomed, 100%' David Walliams accuser tells ITV NewsAsked how she feels about Walliams now, she told the investigation: "I think I was groomed. 100%."Walliams told the publications he believed she was 18 at the time they had sex. The investigation said Alex had joked to Walliams in an email she was "old enough to go drinking", but was actually 17.Walliams denied grooming Alex. He said he is "mortified to learn" that their "brief, consensual relationship has caused her sadness".Jade also alleged she met Walliams when she was 15, in August 2007, in a Soho cafe.Later, at his home, she alleged, he kissed her, lifted up her T-shirt, went on to commit an act that she now characterises as a sexual assault, and tried to put her hand down his trousers. She referred to what happened that night as "unwanted physical touching and emotional manipulation".She said she considers what she says happened to her to have been "grooming", adding: "It's completely wrong in every way."Walliams strongly denied that he had any sexual contact with Jade. He said he rejected any allegations of criminal activity and says he has never engaged in the grooming of young women.Another woman, named as Ella, says she was 19 and working as a model when she rejected Walliams when he tried to kiss her during a tour of his home. She referred to what happened that night as "unwanted physical touching and emotional manipulation".Walliams said he made a "clumsy pass" at Ella, and he made no further approaches. He said he had no intention of intimidating Ella, or making her feel uncomfortable.Other women claimed they were invited to Walliams's dressing room at Britain's Got Talent, or contacted by him after attending a taping. Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Walliams (centre, in 2019) served as a judge for 10 series of ITV's Britain's Got TalentSyco Entertainment, the company that created Britain's Got Talent, said it had had "no knowledge of the allegations described and was not made aware of them at the time".The show's production company, Fremantle UK, said "no complaint has ever been made" against Walliams and encouraged anyone who "feels they have been the subject of any impropriety or wrongdoing by anyone... to come forward".Women who worked for publisher HarperCollins also allege Walliams behaved inappropriately towards younger female employees.One intern at the company told colleagues she had had a consensual sexual relationship with Walliams, but felt it was an "abuse of power".After conducting an internal investigation, HarperCollins announced it was dropping Walliams as an author. Earlier this year, it also said it would no longer be publishing his back catalogue. In a statement responding to ITV News and the Guardian's investigation, the company said it takes employee wellbeing "extremely seriously".Walliams denies that he sexually harassed anyone at HarperCollins or behaved inappropriately in the workplace.Walliams, 55, previously brought legal action against Independent Television News (ITN), which makes ITV News, and Guardian News and Media (GNM), publisher of the Guardian, to try and prevent the claims being published. The two news organisations had argued that they believed it was in the public interest to publish the allegations.Walliams denied the claims and his lawyers said any publication would be "highly likely" to lead him to kill himself, after two previous suicide attempts, and that the court should prevent any publication or broadcast.Last week, a High Court judge rejected the injunction request and Walliams did not lodge an appeal, clearing the way for him to be named.

schema.headline: David Walliams accused of sexual misconduct in Guardian and ITN investigation

title: Met Police investigating more 'potential criminal allegations' about Russell Brand
description: Image source, Getty ImagesByHelena Wilkinson & Paul GlynnBBC NewsUpdated 7 hours agoThe Metropolitan Police have said several people contacted them du
body: Image source, Getty ImagesByHelena Wilkinson & Paul GlynnBBC NewsUpdated 7 hours agoThe Metropolitan Police have said several people contacted them during the trial and following the conviction and sentencing of the disgraced comedian Russell Brand, "to provide information or report a potential criminal allegation".A Met spokesperson said: "Detectives are assessing this information as part of their ongoing enquiries."Speaking to BBC Breakfast, Det Supt Andy Furphy, who led the Brand investigation, said officers were "looking at exactly what we've got" and "whether they're information that points to behaviour or whether they could constitute a criminal offence".Brand is already being investigated over rape allegations from two more women. He has been interviewed under caution in connection to those allegations.On Monday, Brand was sentenced to 10 years and six months in prison, after being convicted of rape and sexual assault.In his sentencing remarks, judge Joel Bennathan described him as a "sexual predator" and criticised his "staggering arrogance".The 51-year-old was sentenced to nine years for rape, with an additional 18 months, nine months and eight months for three counts of sexual assault. The latter sentences are to run concurrently.He was found guilty of the charges involving four women between 2004 and 2009.The head of the Metropolitan Police, Sir Mark Rowley, said on Friday that he "wouldn't be surprised" if more people came forward to make allegations about him.The Downfall of Russell BrandHow the outspoken comedian went from Hollywood stardom to a prison sentence.Asked by BBC Breakfast how the women in the case who gave evidence in the trial were coping, Furphy said: "Some have found it deeply distressing because of the amount of media attention wrapped around it."Even Russell Brand himself before and during trial was putting material online, but we continue to support them."He noted how the conviction "could not have been achieved" without their "bravery, their courage, their resilience throughout the whole criminal justice process".He continued: "It's deeply personal and quite harrowing to be a victim of rape and sexual assault, and to have to tell anybody about it, let alone police officers."But I'm glad they did. I'm glad they put their trust in us."Image source, James Manning/Press AssociationImage caption, Detective Superintendent Andy Furphy speaking to the media outside court after Brand was convictedMP Dame Caroline Dinenage has re-iterated her concerns about Brand being able to post videos online in the build-up to and during his trial to his millions of followers."This does continue to be an issue that he has made money throughout the process on his social media platform," she told the same BBC TV programme."It just felt very odd that during the height of when there was a police investigation and some really serious allegations in the paper, that he was able to go online to his two and a half million followers, denying everything and putting his side of the story forward."That was an opportunity that his victims didn't have."Image source, Elizabeth Cook/Press AssociationImage caption, Brand did not react in the dock as he was sentenced. Before being taken down to the cells, he mouthed "I love you" to his wife Laura Brand, who was in the court.In September 2023, after the Sunday Times and Channel 4 Dispatches allegations were made against Brand, Culture, Media and Sport (CMS) Committee chair Dame Caroline wrote to social media companies Rumble, X, TikTok and Meta.She asked if they would follow YouTube in cutting off Brand's income on their platforms. Rumble publicly refused, and X said it does not take action against accounts that have not broken its rules or the law. TikTok said he had never been monetised there."We know that he had used his following [online] to try and cow people into silence," added Dame Caroline."And the fact that they [the women] were able to come forward and tell their story and tell their truth and secure this conviction because of it is unbelievably impressive."

schema.headline: Met Police investigating more 'potential criminal allegations' about Russell Brand

title: Formula 1: Season to finish in Qatar and Abu Dhabi as planned
description: Formula 1 has told the Imola circuit in Italy that it will not be required as a back-up for the two end-of-season races in the Middle East.The sport i
body: Formula 1 has told the Imola circuit in Italy that it will not be required as a back-up for the two end-of-season races in the Middle East.The sport is pressing ahead with plans to hold the two events in Qatar on 27-29 November and Abu Dhabi in the United Arab Emirates on 4-6 December, despite the ongoing conflict between the United States/Israel and Iran.Imola had been asked to prepare for a potential grand prix on the Abu Dhabi dates if the two Middle Eastern races could not go ahead.Imola was asked on Tuesday to stand down preparations - but F1 says that if the situation in the Middle East deteriorates it is still prepared to cancel the two races.Earlier in the season, races in Saudi Arabia and Bahrain, both of which had been scheduled for April, were cancelled and delayed respectively following the outbreak of the United States and Israel's war with Iran.The Bahrain Grand Prix was eventually held at Malaysia's Sepang circuit in October."If the situation develops negatively in the coming weeks before the events in the Middle East, we will not hesitate to do the right thing and the safety of everyone will always be the priority," an F1 spokesperson said on Tuesday.F1 says the decision to press ahead with Qatar and Abu Dhabi, which was always the default option, has been taken because the situation in the two countries has not "negatively developed" in recent months.Travel advice from governments still allows travel, insurance is valid, events are taking place and business has returned to a normal level in both countries, it said, adding that the teams are all supportive of concluding the season as planned.A MotoGP race was held in Qatar last weekend. That sport is owned by the same US group that owns F1.Despite the decision, a number of senior figures in F1 have expressed disquiet to BBC Sport about the idea of going to the Middle East for the races, as both are close to areas in the Straight of Hormuz where missile strikes are still taking place.And Saudi Arabia continues to be the target of attacks from Houthi rebels in Yemen.Several events in Saudi Arabia, which borders Qatar and the United Arab Emirates, have been cancelled or postponed in recent weeks following those attacks.However, there is recognition that F1 faces a difficult decision. The two countries pay large fees for their events, and both are heavily ingrained in the fabric of the sports as sponsors and investors.The Qatari sovereign investment fund, for example, is a part owner of the Audi team, and Abu Dhabi is the same for McLaren.

schema.headline: Formula 1: Season to finish in Qatar and Abu Dhabi as planned

title: Analysis: Hegseth fights for his political life with appeal to Trump
description: There was plenty of defiance and rhetorical venom from Pete Hegseth at the Pentagon on Tuesday, as the under-pressure US defence secretary gave his fi
body: There was plenty of defiance and rhetorical venom from Pete Hegseth at the Pentagon on Tuesday, as the under-pressure US defence secretary gave his first news conference in six months.Much of his ire was directed at the Republican Congressman Thomas Massie, who has brought articles of impeachment against him. Hegseth dismissed him as "one disgruntled and defeated congressman" who was leading a "farce and a stunt".But this was, in many ways, a news conference with an audience of one - President Donald Trump.Again and again, Hegseth tied his fate to that of the president.The military operations in Iran and Venezuela that are now at the centre of impeachment proceedings, he said, were "ordered by the commander-in-chief, then ordered by myself". If standing with the president put him in the firing line, he added, "I'll take that company every day of the week".That positioning matters.Hegseth has frequently echoed the president's rhetoric and public statements and he did it repeatedly on Tuesday. Attacks on the media, denunciations of political enemies and even reflecting the very words the president uses.Referring to Trump's 2019 impeachment over a call with Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky, Hegseth described it as a "perfect phone call" – the exact formulation the president has used when discussing the issue.All of this leaves this president with an impossible dilemma.If he opts to keep his defence secretary, it risks looking as though he has not heard the message from voters. Fire him, and it risks looking like an admission that the Iran war has become a damaging domestic liability.A scalp or a scapegoat, put it how you like, may be necessary if Trump is to move on.Even the promotion of Stephen Miller to White House chief-of-staff provides less comfort than it might appear. He and Hegseth are close allies, and Hegseth today called him an "incredible American patriot".But Miller reportedly clinched the job after arguing that the White House needed to wind down the Iran war – putting a clear level of distance between the Pentagon and the president.For the time being, Hegseth has the president's backing – but as everyone knows in Washington. a full-throated endorsement from Trump can, in the blink of an eye, evaporate into nothing if a sacrifice is required.Votes in Congress will be the focus on Tuesday as impeachment proceedings against Hegseth get under way. But in reality, it is the president's feelings that will likely be the ultimate arbiter of Hegseth's political fate.

schema.headline: Analysis: Hegseth fights for his political life with appeal to Trump

title: Anthropic set for $1.3tn stock market debut despite 'catastrophic' AI warning
description: Anthropic, the artificial intelligence (AI) company behind the Claude chatbot, could be valued at around $1.3 trillion (£1 trillion) when it lists its
body: Anthropic, the artificial intelligence (AI) company behind the Claude chatbot, could be valued at around $1.3 trillion (£1 trillion) when it lists its shares for sale on New York's Nasdaq stock exchange.The loss-making company says it will offer its shares for between $70 and $78 each and will raise up to $64bn when it floats this month.It would value Anthropic at between $1.1tn and $1.3tn which, although large, is below the $2tn some backers of the firm predicted in summer, according to the Financial Times.The huge valuation comes despite the company warning last month that AI could pose "catastrophic or existential risks to humanity".It is floating at a volatile time for big tech firms. After last week's US midterm elections, the Nasdaq fell sharply on concerns a Democrat-led Congress could slow development of AI and the buildout of data centres.There are also wider fears over the billions of dollars being spent on AI and whether it will pay off.In its most recent results for the six months to the end of June, Anthropic's revenues jumped to $16.2bn from $1.1bn in the same period last year. However, its pre-tax loss jumped to $80.7bn from $12.9bn.Fiona Cincotta, a senior market analyst at City Index, said the $64bn Anthropic wants to raise is "fairly bullish" within "the volatility [and] concerns towards AI that we've seen in sort of particularly last week".She told Reuters: "It's showing that they are still sort of upbeat about the outlook as far as AI is concerned and that obviously that they think that the demand is going to be there."Anthropic, which will list under the symbol ANT on 19 November, will be the first fully AI-focused company to go public, making it a test case for the future of the technology.At $1.3tn, Anthropic's possible valuation is below SpaceX, Elon Musk's rocket, satellite and artificial intelligence company, which listed its shares in June and was valued at nearly $1.8tn.Anthropic is just five years old. It was co-founded in 2021 by brother and sister Dario and Daniela Amodei along with five others – all of whom worked at OpenAI, the rival AI giant behind ChatGPT.It announced its intention to list on the stock market in June and OpenAI followed suit. That listing is now expected to occur early next year.The listing announcements were followed by a series of incidents involving AI agents, which are bots designed to operate somewhat autonomously, going rogue.Current and former staff of both companies have warned AI technology was being developed without the ability to protect humanity from possible future harms enacted by AI.Anthropic has admitted that advanced AI systems "could, if not developed, deployed, and operated with appropriate safeguards, oversight, and security measures, pose catastrophic or existential risks to humanity, particularly if such systems were misused, replicated, weaponised, or allowed to operate with a high degree of autonomy".The company has reiterated promises to develop AI to be beneficial to people.It has warned investors its future success depends largely on its ability to develop the most advanced AI models, and that "any failure to do so could adversely affect our business".

schema.headline: Anthropic set for $1.3tn stock market debut despite 'catastrophic' AI warning

title: Anti-gay laws in Trinidad and Tobago overturned
description: A UK court has overturned laws criminalising same-sex intimacy in Trinidad and Tobago.London's Judicial Committee of the Privy Council (JCPC), the Car
body: A UK court has overturned laws criminalising same-sex intimacy in Trinidad and Tobago.London's Judicial Committee of the Privy Council (JCPC), the Caribbean island's final court of appeal, ruled the laws were not in keeping with the "fundamental individual right to respect for private and family life."The judgement is the result of an 11-year legal battle brought by dual-citizen Jason Jones, 62, who said he hoped it would "accelerate the fight for full equality."Jones had successfully challenged the laws in 2018 in Trinidad's High Court, however the ruling was overturned on appeal by the Trinidadian government.It is the first time the JCPC has ever decided on a case to decriminalise same-sex intimacy, and campaigners hope it will spark similar successful legal challenges elsewhere in the Commonwealth.Prior to this historic decision, Trinidad and Tobago was one of some 34 Commonwealth countries continuing to criminalise homosexuality based on colonial-era British laws. Under these laws, consensual same-sex intimacy is punishable by imprisonment, and in some cases carries the death penalty.The Attorney General of Trinidad and Tobago had argued that the law was protected from legal challenges by the "savings law clauses" - which carried over existing British laws into newly independent states.Representatives for Jones argued that the laws violated an individual's right to privacy and argued the government's changes to the laws in 1986 - which saw stricter punishments introduced - meant the savings clause protections no longer applied.The judicial committee unanimously found in favour of Jones.Handing down the judgement, Lord Sales told the court the laws "cannot be regarded as reasonably justifiable in a society that has a proper respect for the rights and freedoms of an individual".Jones, human rights campaigner and appellant in the appeal, said: "These laws never reflected who we are as a people and a nation - diverse, multiracial, and secular. "They told LGBTQ+ people that we were criminals in our own country. That message ends today."Lawyer Anand Ramlogan SC, representing Jones, said the judgement was a "landmark victory for gay rights, equal dignity and respect for private and family life in Trinidad and Tobago."

schema.headline: Anti-gay laws in Trinidad and Tobago overturned

title: Nvidia hires major New York law firm to investigate Jensen Huang affair
description: Nvidia has hired New York law firm Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz to investigate the affair between its chief executive and an alleged Chinese spy.Jen
body: Nvidia has hired New York law firm Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz to investigate the affair between its chief executive and an alleged Chinese spy.Jensen Huang, a co-founder of Nvidia who has led it to become one of the most valuable companies in the world, admitted to having a romantic relationship with a woman outside of his marriage.The woman, Alice Huang, is alleged to be a spy for Beijing. She was an executive at a Singaporean company Megaspeed, which has been a customer of Nvidia.Nvidia said on Tuesday that Wachtell attorney Joon Kim was set to lead "a thorough and independent investigation" into Jensen Huang's affair. The FBI is also conducting its own probe.Nvidia is widely considered one of the most important companies behind the US artificial intelligence (AI) boom given it is the sole manufacturer of a crucial computer chip required for successfully operating AI tools.Shares in the company fell to a near-yearly low on Tuesday, wiping more than $500bn (£375bn) off Nvidia's stock market value since Friday, even as tech stocks have recovered since last week's sell-off. Jensen Huang's relationship with an executive of an Nvidia customer, who is also believed by the US government to be spying for China, has business and national security implications.Megaspped had been suspected of helping divert Nvidia chips to China, a concern that Nvidia has maintained was investigated and debunked.According to the New York Times, Secretary of State Marco Rubio sent a memo to top officials in Washington in spring of this year warning that the Nvidia boss was in a close relationship with a Chinese spy.Beijing has rejected claims that Jensen Huang has been targeted, with its foreign ministry saying the allegations were "intended to smear and malign China".US President Donald Trump said Monday that he had spoken to Jensen Huang and that the Nvidia boss told him "I had no idea she was a spy." Trump said he believed the him.When announcing on Sunday that it would investigate the affair, Nvidia's board said it had no reason to believe the company's secrets or national security were compromised.However, the relationship has drawn political attention. Congressional leaders of the House Committee on Foreign Affairs have asked Jensen Huang to appear next week for a closed door briefing. The Nvidia boss has yet to say whether he will attend, a person familiar with the committee's demand told the BBC. Committee chair congressman Brian Mast said he would subpoena Jensen Huang, effectively forcing him to appear before the committee, if necessary.Joon Kim, who will lead Nvidia's investigation, is a former US Attorney for New York's Southern District and spent several years working as a government attorney focused on fraud and other criminal acts.Wachtell is one of the largest law firms in the US and has several notable clients in the tech industry. Among them are OpenAI and Salesforce.The investigation is expected to be treated as urgent, according to sources familiar with the sentiment inside Nvidia. It is unclear, however, if Wachtell will be able to interview Alice Huang, who is also known as Huang Le, and is not related to Jensen Huang.Jensen Huang's public image is tightly intertwined with Nvidia. He has become a key public figure in the devleopment on AI, arguing the technology is a "new industrial revolution" and is on par with the advent of electricity.A spokesperson for Nvidia declined to comment on Tuesday when asked if Jensen Huang had retained any additional of his own legal representation amid the company investigation and the separate one launched by the FBI.

schema.headline: Nvidia hires major New York law firm to investigate Jensen Huang affair

title: French wartime resistance heroine Solange Alexandre dies aged 104
description: One of France's last Resistance heroes from World War Two has died at the age of 104.  Solange Alexandre was also a rare woman who, with her future hu
body: One of France's last Resistance heroes from World War Two has died at the age of 104.  Solange Alexandre was also a rare woman who, with her future husband, created and commanded her own unit of anti-German fighters.After serving as a Resistance courier from 1941, three years later she founded the Pas-de-Boeuf network near the town of Ruillé-sur-Loir.With some 30 men under her orders, she organised sabotage operations, sheltered Allied airmen and, after the Allied landings in Normandy on D-Day in 1944, joined the fight against the occupying German forces.President Emmanuel Macron was among many to pay tribute to Alexandre, after her death was announced at a nursing home in Le Mans."She said she only ever did her duty. But her duty was our freedom. France will never forget. Thank you," Macron posted on social media.Born in 1922 in the Sarthe department of western France,  Solange Alexandre, née Dubuisson, grew up in a patriotic family that had suffered in World War One."My mother lost her first husband in the war, and my father was wounded in 1917.   The words homeland and honour were very important to us. They were in my blood," she recalled in her memoirs.In June 1940 she heard on the radio the appeal from General Charles de Gaulle in London, calling on the French not to give up the struggle against Germany.  She had never heard of him, but that did not matter."From that moment I knew I had to join up," she wrote.Some months later she was recruited by a friend of her father's – a Tunisian-born French army veteran called Saïd Belhaffaf, who had joined the Resistance.Using the code-name Corlay, she criss-crossed the region around Le Mans by bicycle, gathering information and passing on messages."There were no mobile phones back then, and no private cars either because of the lack of petrol. The bicycle was king," she said in an interview two years ago.In 1943 she met her first husband Guy Déliot, who had deserted from the French gendarmerie after refusing to arrest some Jews.The following April, with the Allied invasion approaching, they decided to take to the maquis, in other words live clandestinely in the forested hills, supplied with food by local farmers.Their group consisted of deserters from German forced labour programmes, as well as survivors from another Resistance outfit that had been destroyed by the enemy.  There were also two airmen, one American and one Canadian."Twice the Gestapo came for me, and twice I slipped through their hands," she later recalled.After taking part in the liberation of Tours in September 1944, she ended the war with the rank of sub-lieutenant in the French Interior Forces (FFI).Later she worked as a teacher and followed her husband on his many postings as an officer of the gendarmerie in French overseas territories. He was killed in 1960 in Martinique, and in 1981 she remarried.Twice Solange Alexandre turned down the Légion d'Honneur, saying that she had only done her duty and that others were more worthy. Finally in 2024 she relented.On receiving the award she said: "It is a great pleasure and a great honour.  I am very proud – even if it is only a few weeks, or a few months, before I die."

schema.headline: French wartime resistance heroine Solange Alexandre dies aged 104

title: Manchester United: Michael Carrick future to be discussed at Monaco meeting
description: The Monaco summit that will decide the future of Carrick and Man UtdImage source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Manchester United minority owner Sir Jim
body: The Monaco summit that will decide the future of Carrick and Man UtdImage source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Manchester United minority owner Sir Jim Ratcliffe (left), chief executive Omar Berrada (centre) and director of football Jason Wilcox will decide Michael Carrick's fate as head coachMichael Carrick's future as Manchester United head coach will be determined 800 miles away from Old Trafford in Monaco on Wednesday.Chief executive Omar Berrada and director of football Jason Wilcox are flying out for one of their regular pre-planned meetings to discuss strategy around the football club.On this occasion, the main issue to be decided is Carrick's future and what should happen next.It is expected that Berrada and Wilcox's recommendation is for the head coach to go.It is not a situation Sir Jim Ratcliffe can have expected to find himself in again, less than three years after purchasing a minority stake in United.On Christmas Eve 2023, his vision was much different."Our shared ambition is clear: we all want to see Manchester United back where we belong, at the very top of English, European and world football," he said.Instead, United are 18th, in the Premier League's relegation zone after winning just one of their first 10 games and none since August. It is their lowest position so far into a top-flight season since 1986-87 when they were 20th.Ratcliffe has been criticised for many decisions since he bought his 28.94% stake for just over £1bn. This is one he really needs to get right.Figure caption, How close is Carrick to Man United exit?Why is the meeting taking place in Monaco?Ratcliffe's home is in Monaco and his company Ineos has offices in the principality.The meeting had been in the diary for some time as a regular catch-up between senior executives and their boss.Sources have stressed that the choice of location was not influenced by the debate around Carrick's future - it just happens to now be the most important item for discussion.The decision to sack United's previous two managers was not made in a meeting in Monaco.Ruben Amorim was sacked 19 hours after his explosive media conference following a 1-1 draw at Leeds in January. Erik ten Hag went a day after Manchester United lost at West Ham leaving them with just three wins from their opening nine matchesA decision to sack Dutchman Ten Hag was taken at a meeting of senior Ineos executives in the summer of 2024, only for the choice to be reversed following the FA Cup final triumph over Manchester City.Four months later there was a six-hour meeting at Ineos HQ in London as Ten Hag's tenure hung by a thread. He survived again but was gone three weeks later.Amorim was summoned to Monaco after the Europa League final defeat to Tottenham in 2025.There is daily contact between senior executives so if the meeting was purely to decide Carrick's fate, it could be done by video conference and the need to travel to Monaco is not the reason why there is yet to be a decision.The travel element does add a complication given the preference for Berrada and Wilcox is to inform Carrick of any decision face to face. Sources say the Monaco meetings used to be held every six weeks, although in more recent times they are less frequent.Those who have attended them say they take place in the morning, tend to last between three and four hours and usually stop on time so Ratcliffe can go for his regular lunchtime jog.What do we know about the recommendation to sack Carrick?Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Carrick won 12 games out of 17 as interim boss to earn a two-year contract as Manchester United head coach in the summerUnited stood by Carrick after the woeful 3-0 home defeat by Bournemouth on 25 October. Club sources were adamant they wanted to give Carrick and his players a chance to turn the situation around it was also felt that the two-week international break in November represented a better chance for the club to properly assess the club's start to the campaign.However, although they did end a long wait for a victory against Roma on 3 November, United had to come from two goals down to seal a 3-2 victory in a chaotic game. They failed to press home their advantage after excelling in the first half against Chelsea and eventually lost 2-0 as experienced central defender Lisandro Martinez was sent off. On Sunday, they conceded twice inside five minutes and had to come from two goals down twice to claim a point against Villa.While sources said the comebacks showed the United squad were still playing for Carrick, it is also understood the chaotic nature of the games and the inability to stop the opposition from scoring has led Berrada and Wilcox, who were at all three matches, to conclude a change of coach is required to get United out of the mess they find themselves in.United have conceded 30 goals so far this season in 15 games - 19 in 10 Premier League matches, eight in four in the Champions League and three in their one Carabao Cup tie.Instead of replacing Carrick another option under consideration is additional coaching support to assist the current team.Bayern Munich coach Aaron Danks, who worked with Carrick at Middlesbrough and was touted as a potential appointment in the summer, is one option.Is the recommendation likely to be accepted?Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Manchester United co-chair Avram Glazer (left) with minority owner Sir Jim Ratcliffe at the 2025 Europa League finalThe assumption is yes. If Ratcliffe was to decide otherwise, it would raise serious questions over the future of Berrada and Wilcox.How could they work with Carrick again in that scenario?The pair have been the subject of intense and frequent fan discontent. But sources are adamant that Ratcliffe still retains faith in the pair, even though United are heading towards sacking a manager in mid-season for the third successive year, having backed them in the summer and spend millions on new players.Ratcliffe is a ruthless operator, and has clear opinions of his own. He also has form, spending £5m hiring Dan Ashworth as sporting director from Newcastle in 2024, then waiting for the 55-year-old to spend five months on gardening leave before he could start work. Five months later, Ashworth was sacked due to a divergence of opinion over who should replace Ten Hag. Ashworth felt someone with Premier League experience was a better fit for United's squad. Ratcliffe wanted a more modern alternative. Berrada suggested Amorim. Wilcox, after initial reservations, also got on board. Amorim was dismissed after 14 months.The other unknown element is the Glazer family. They will need to sign off any decision.At the time of the Ratcliffe purchase, United confirmed the club's 'board' had handed over responsibility for the football side. But United's articles of association state that responsibilities delegated by directors can also be "revoked or altered". Crucially, of the 12 current directors, six are members of the Glazer family, including co-chairs Joel and Avi Glazer. United's rules state that if required, the chairman of any meeting will have a second and casting vote.Although there have been media reports of Glazer dissatisfaction at United's current plight, there has been no public statement on the matter.What is Carrick scheduled to be doing for the next couple of days?It may seem strange, but the reality is, as with any employee, Carrick will continue to do his job until told otherwise - and so far, there has been no conversation to that effect.Although most of his squad, and a significant number of academy players, are on international duty, a core remains at home. This includes Mason Mount, Joshua Zirkzee and Matthijs de Ligt. Harry Maguire, who suffered a back spasm against Villa, is also there, as are other injured players, including Luke Shaw and Marcus Rashford.Carrick gave his players a day off on Monday but scheduled training days for Tuesday, Wednesday and Thursday. After that, they are not due to report back until 17 November, by which time the international contingent should start to return and begin preparations for the trip to Liverpool on 22 November."Obviously some of the boys will be flying off around the world and different things, and the group will be split for 10 days or so, but as a normal international week is, we'll have some training and we'll have one or two days off," Carrick said after the Villa game. "Not too much. But we'll train and get ready for the next game."Who might be discussed as a possible replacement for Carrick?Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Mauricio Pochettino was appointed USA boss in September 2024If the discussions go as anticipated, replacing Carrick will be a key element.Mauricio Pochettino has emerged as a leading contender and is known to be keen on the job.United spoke to the former Tottenham, PSG and Chelsea boss about their managerial position on three different occasions - first of all when Jose Mourinho was sacked in 2018, then in 2022 when the club decided on Ten Hag instead and then again when the Dutchman was sacked. The obvious problem is that Pochettino currently has a job as head coach of the United States. He renewed his contract in August and has a two-legged Concacaf Nations League quarter-final against Haiti over the next week. The Argentine, 54, is due to speak to the media on Friday and has a $10m (£7.5m) release clause.Former Newcastle boss Eddie Howe is out of work and available. BBC Sport has reported the compensation due to his old club if Manchester United appointed thr 48-year-old now would be £3m. But it reduces as the season goes on and would be nothing in the summer.Italian Antonio Conte is also thought to be keen and the 57-year-old has Premier League title-winning experience at Chelsea and more recently won Serie A with Napoli last season, before leaving the club. Julian Nagelsmann stood down as Germany boss in the wake of their last-32 exit at the World Cup exit at the World Cup but the German, 39, won the Bundesliga title with Bayern Munich in 2022-23. Kieran McKenna was part of Ole Gunnar Solskjaer's coaching team at Manchester United and left Ipswich after four-and-a-half years this summer. However, it is felt more likely United would want a candidate with greater experience than the 40-year-old Northern Irishman.Where does this all leave Carrick? In a unenviable position of carrying on as if it was business as usual when the reality is anything but.Follow Manchester United on BBC SoundsPre-match, post-match and topical United contentSubscribe and listen for everything you love about the Red Devils

title: Inside devastated front-line city of Slovyansk that Russia wants Ukraine to give up
description: Figure caption, Meet the Peaky Blinders, Ukraine's drone unit protecting devastated front-line cityByJonathan Beale Defence correspondentReporting fro
body: Figure caption, Meet the Peaky Blinders, Ukraine's drone unit protecting devastated front-line cityByJonathan Beale Defence correspondentReporting fromSlovyansk, eastern UkraineThe dangers in Slovyansk are clear from the start."If I say run, you run," Tetiana tells us. She and her colleague Yasha are escorting us into a city now under constant bombardment from Russian drones, missiles and glide bombs.It is raining and cloudy as we enter the city, and our military escorts call this "good" weather, meaning it is bad for drones.But the threat is still there, and Yasha keeps his eyes peeled on the skies, while 21-year-old Tetiana scours her phone for the latest military intelligence on likely threats from the air. They are members of a drone unit who call themselves Peaky Blinders and their distinctive emblem is a flat cap of the type made popular by the cult BBC TV series, although theirs are camouflaged.Slovyansk is one of four cities that make up Ukraine's "fortress belt" - a system of heavily reinforced defence lines in the parts of eastern region of Donetsk still under its control.Russia wants Kyiv to give up the fortress cities and they are central to talks on a possible peace deal that have resumed after nine months between Ukraine, Russia and the US in Abu Dhabi.Ukrainians worry that doing so would make it much easier for Russia to advance further west, including to the capital Kyiv.Image source, BBC/Moose CampbellImage caption, Very little of the city has been left unscathed by months of heavy bombardmentOnce inside the city, we leave our vehicles hidden under the cover of trees and venture out on foot. Yasha carries a shotgun – a last resort to shoot down Russian drones. In halting English, Tetiana tells us walking is safer than travelling by car.Abandoned vehicles litter the streets – recently destroyed by remotely operated Russian first-person view drones. The anti-drone netting that covers the roads is no guarantee of safety.Tetiana shows us a video on her phone taken a few days earlier.You can hear several drones buzzing above her, and then the cacophony of small arms fire as Ukrainian forces try to shoot them down. Tetiana admits it can be scary but explains how she felt compelled to help her country, abandoning her dreams of becoming an opera singer.Slovyansk is now a husk of its former self. Very few buildings have been left unscathed, with many reduced to rubble.Tetiana shows us a school recently destroyed by Russian glide bombs. Across the road there is a gaping hole in an abandoned residential block. Broken glass litters the pavement. The few shops still functioning are boarded up – making it hard to distinguish what is still open. Most have closed.Tetiana says the Russians are doing everything they can to intimidate people and drive them out of the city. That, she says, "is their strategy – to make people leave in chaos, gathering up their last belongings and fleeing amid enormous fear and suffering. They want people to have nowhere left to live".It is a familiar pattern already seen in other Ukrainian towns and cities in the Donbas – like Pokrovsk and Bakhmut. These are now ghost towns reduced to rubble, but eventually falling into Russian hands.Russia has already taken nearly 90% of the Donbas – made up of the regions of Luhansk and Donetsk - but its advances this year have all but stalled in the face of strong Ukrainian resistance.The White House is sounding positive about the revived talks in Abu Dhabi, despite Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky's refusal to cede the territory.October was the deadliest month for Russian troops since the start of its full-scale invasion – with more than 54,000 killed or injured, according to Ukraine's general staff. Despite this, Russian forces are still making life in the Fortress Belt cities almost impossible.Image source, BBC/Moose CampbellImage caption, Iryna, who works in one of the city's last remaining cafes, is one of the few residents who decided to stayBefore the war, Slovyansk was a city of more than 200,000 people. Less than 10% of those remain and the population diminishes by the day.But amid the wail of near constant air raid warnings, there are still signs of people clinging on to life here. Iryna works in one of the city's last remaining coffee shops. Slovyansk is where she was born."I'm forced to walk around crying," she tells me. "How can they do this?"Life, she says, has become incredibly difficult. She has already lost her house. But despite her tears, there is still defiance: "I won't leave Slovyansk. This is my home."Inga, 53, was also born and raised here and continues to work in the city despite the danger.  "It's stressful. Honestly, I don't even know what to say," she says, but she is staying because of what she calls the "fear of the unknown"."I simply have nowhere to go, and I don't have the money to leave or support myself afterwards." Nor, she says, is there anywhere else in Ukraine she would consider truly safe.Image source, BBC/Moose CampbellImage caption, Commander Oleksandr of the Peaky Blinders special forces unit says neither side is able to advance because of the large number of drones in useWe first met the Omega National Guard Special Forces drone unit two years ago fighting in the Kharkiv region, in north-eastern Ukraine.Just four of the original team remain - the rest have moved to other units, or they have been wounded or killed.Among the dead was the brother of the man in charge of the unit, Oleksandr, who now describes his unit as his family.He jokes it is just like the Peaky Blinders TV show – "but without the crime and the drugs". Back at their base they share a meal every evening.Oleksandr reads out a prayer of thanks for surviving another day – he says it strengthens their spirits. The meal is accompanied by classical music played on a speaker. It helps drown out the noise of the explosions nearby."I feel this is the most difficult situation we've ever faced," says Oleksandr, who underlines the importance of holding the line."We must be here to inflict maximum damage on the enemy. We're fighting here because this is where the most intense phase of the war is taking place. Russia's claim that they will reach the borders of the Donbas, seize it, and then the war will end is absolutely false," he insists.The remaining fortress belt cities provide Ukraine with a strong defensive line and are a major obstacle to any Russian advance. The saturation of drones in the area is also now making it nigh-on impossible for either side to advance here.Peace talks may have resumed, but Oleksandr notes they have not led to anything so far."I really want this war to end," he says, "but do I believe these negotiations will succeed? No, I don't really believe they will".Image source, EPAImage caption, The streets are largely empty, with increasing numbers of residents evacuated as drone attacks intensifyThe next morning we are not the only ones making an exit. A dozen civilians have arrived at an evacuation point in the centre to be escorted out.They hold all the belongings they can carry and are taken into a bunker for their safety. Outside there is another heavy blast of small arms fire, signalling more drones are nearby.Alina Shyrko, herself a resident of Slovyansk, is co-ordinating the move of civilians out of the city and says the situation has deteriorated rapidly over the past few months. Families with children have already been ordered to leave.  "Everyone is thinking about leaving," she says, "I'm thinking about it too."Ukraine still holds Slovyansk but its lifeblood, its people, are ebbing away.Additional reporting by Rebecca Hartmann, Volodymyr Lozhko and Moose Campbell.

schema.headline: Inside devastated front-line city of Slovyansk that Russia wants Ukraine to give up

title: US federal authorities could have prevented Epstein crimes, report finds
description: Regarding Epstein's death in a New York prison, investigators concluded this was a result of "a series of institutional failures at the facility," whi
body: Regarding Epstein's death in a New York prison, investigators concluded this was a result of "a series of institutional failures at the facility," which included staffing shortages, overworked employees, poor recordkeeping, and lax security practices.  Testimony the panel solicited was "unable to definitively dispel certain theories" surrounding Epstein's death, the report states, including accounting for a lapse in surveillance footage.It found the justice department (DoJ) failed to communicate about document releases and that deficient redactions exposed survivors' sensitive personal information.The DoJ has released millions of pages of Epstein-related files in response to legislation from Congress.Earlier this year, the department had to remove thousands of documents related to Epstein from its website after victims said their identities had been compromised.The report also alleges that financial institutions like American Express enabled human trafficking and immigration fraud, by allowing Epstein to use decoy flights and dummy itineraries to transport foreign workers across borders. The BBC has contacted American Express for comment. The investigative panel recommended that Congress should pass legislation to prevent the weaponisation of non-disclosure agreements, which they said Epstein used to silence survivors."Epstein operated with impunity, shielded and enabled by powerful connections and a justice system that repeatedly failed his victims," said James Comer, the Republican chairman of the committee. He called upon the DoJ to "interview or re-interview key witnesses, investigate Epstein associates accused of criminal activity, and ensure survivors have access to their records.The department remains under bipartisan scruntiny regarding the Epstein files.In the state of New Mexico, where Epstein had a ranch, the top state prosecutor accused the DoJ of stonewalling their criminal investigation."With all due respect, the Chairman's recommendations have already been addressed," a spokesperson for the department said in response to Comer's report."The Attorney General has repeatedly said that the Epstein case is not closed and there is no statute of limitations on human trafficking."The report accuses Democrats of being "obsessed" with trying to implicate US President Donald Trump and that an "unfounded witch hunt continued without regard for the interests of survivors".Trump has previously said he was friendly with Epstein before they fell out in 2004. The president's name has appeared thousands of times in the Epstein files but there is no suggestion that appearing in the documents implies any wrongdoing. The committee's review of documents did not identify any that would implicate Trump, the report concluded.In a statement, Rep Robert Garcia, the top Democrat on the Oversight Committee, alleged his Republican colleagues "released a report based on an incomplete investigation and zero public hearings on Jeffrey Epstein".Garcia accused the justice department of withholding "over 2.5 million pages of documents"."We will not allow the President and his allies to dismiss this investigation," said Garcia, who is expected to lead the committee when Democrats take control of Congress in January following the recent midterm elections. The family members of one of Epstein's most prominent accusers, the late Virginia Roberts Giuffre, thanked Comer for releasing Tuesday's report."A sentence from the report stands out to us: 'Questions remain as to whether the DOJ has released all its relevant documents.' We could not agree more and urge that all 7 million-plus files be released," Sky and Amanda Roberts said in a statement."There are many more individuals who have yet to be identified and brought to justice," they said.

schema.headline: US federal authorities could have prevented Epstein crimes, report finds

title: Who is David Walliams? His career and controversies including Little Britain and BGT
description: David Walliams has been accused of grooming young fans and harassing women in the workplace, after failing to stop the Guardian and ITN publishing cla
body: David Walliams has been accused of grooming young fans and harassing women in the workplace, after failing to stop the Guardian and ITN publishing claims against him.A three-year investigation, external by the two news organisations alleged the Little Britain star and former Britain's Got Talent judge preyed on teenage girls as young as 15 and young women, external for sexual purposes.He had sought a High Court injunction to prevent publication, with his lawyers arguing if allegations were made public Walliams would likely kill himself. The court refused the request.Walliams has denied all of the allegations but in a letter to journalists working on the investigation acknowledged "at times I behaved thoughtlessly towards other people I had casual sexual relationships with".He added: "I am not a sexual predator. I have not broken the law, but I am devastated that some of the women I met 10 to 20 years ago have now expressed hurt or anger towards me."The 55-year-old became a household name in the early 2000s through Little Britain, his comedy sketch show with Matt Lucas broadcast on the BBC.Walliams published his first children's book, The Boy in the Dress, in 2008, and his stories soon became best-sellers and led to comparisons with Roald Dahl.His 23 children's books have sold more than 50 million copies worldwide, but he was dropped by publisher HarperCollins in 2025 after allegations of inappropriate behaviour, which he denied.In 2012, Walliams became a judge on Britain's Got Talent, and was voted best TV judge at the National TV Awards (NTAs) four times. He was replaced as a judge in 2022.Before entering showbusiness, Walliams was born David Williams but changed his surname's spelling to avoid having the same name as another member of entertainment union Equity.He was married to Dutch model Lara Stone from 2010 to 2015 and they have a son.That hasn't stopped speculation about Walliams' sexuality. He has described himself as "bi-curious" and called his 2012 autobiography Camp David – but said he isn't attracted to men in the way he is to women.Not all the criticisms of Walliams have involved new standards being applied to older work.Walliams had to apologise after two charity performances, during which he yanked down not only the trousers but also the underwear of actor Jeremy Edwards and music producer Mark Ronson.In 2020, he was booed while hosting the NTAs after making a joke about Caroline Flack being out of work, at a time when she had stepped down from hosting Love Island and was waiting to appear in court, having been charged for actual bodily harm following a row with her boyfriend.Later in 2022, he was replaced as a judge on Britain's Got Talent after a Guardian story about a leaked recording of Walliams making insulting remarks about contestants during breaks from filming.In the incident, which happened in 2020, he spoke about a pensioner to whom he had taken a strong dislike and a woman who he described as "the slightly boring girl you would meet in the pub" who "you would want to have sex with, but then decide not to". He used much stronger language when talking about both.Walliams apologised, explaining: "These were private conversations and - like most conversations with friends - were never intended to be shared. Nevertheless, I am sorry."He sued the show's producers Freemantle for misuse of his private information and breaching data protection laws. An "amicable resolution" was reached, with the production company apologising for the recording being made public.Further controversy came in June 2025, when it emerged that Walliams had given two Nazi salutes during the recording of BBC One's Would I Lie to You? Christmas special.Banijay UK, which owned the show's production company Zeppotron, apologised, adding: "It was immediately acknowledged during the recording that this segment would not be broadcast under any circumstances." Walliams has never commented on the incident.Then in December 2025, HarperCollins, the publisher of his hugely successful children's books, announced that following a change of CEO, the company would no longer look after new releases by Walliams.He was dropped over allegations he had harassed female members of staff, with HarperCollins explaining that the company took "employee wellbeing extremely seriously and has processes in place for reporting and investigating concerns".The Daily Telegraph reported that an internal investigation had been opened the previous year after a complaint was made by a junior member of staff about his behaviour. This reportedly found that staff had been told to only meet Walliams in pairs and advised against going to his house.Walliams' spokesperson responded by saying he "strongly denies that he has behaved inappropriately" and that he had "never been informed of any allegations raised against him" by the publisher.Then in September 2026, HarperCollins doubled down by announcing that they were cutting all ties with Walliams and would no longer represent his back catalogue, meaning that when his books sold out in shops, they would not be replaced.

schema.headline: Who is David Walliams? His career and controversies including Little Britain and BGT
